name: United States
tagline: Four years, no fixed major on day one, and the widest price range on earth
summary: An American bachelor's degree takes four years and starts broad: you take courses across several fields and usually declare a major at the end of year two. Admission is 'holistic' - your grades matter most, but so do essays, teacher references, what you do outside school, and increasingly again the SAT or ACT. As a Danish student you are an international applicant everywhere, so you pay the published sticker price unless a university gives you financial aid, and only a handful of universities give internationals enough aid to make it affordable. The cost range is enormous: from roughly 40,000 USD a year at a public university to over 95,000 USD a year at a private one.
whyConsider: You do not have to choose your subject before you arrive - you can start in autumn 2027 and declare a major in 2029.
A small group of very wealthy private universities and liberal arts colleges will meet 100% of your assessed financial need, including flights, no matter what your family earns.
Good HL results often convert into real course credit, which can let you skip introductory courses or even finish early.
Liberal arts colleges are small (1,500-2,500 students), taught by professors rather than teaching assistants, and are often more generous to internationals than the famous research universities.
Research, internships and campus jobs are built into the undergraduate experience in a way that is rare in Europe.
watchOuts: Sticker price. Harvard's published billed cost for 2025-26 was 86,926 USD for one year, and that is before health insurance and flights.
Most universities are need-aware for internationals: asking for money reduces your chance of getting in. Only a very short list is need-blind for non-Americans.
The testing landscape flipped back. Harvard and Yale both require the SAT or ACT again for autumn 2027 entry, and IB results do not substitute for the test at Yale.

Deadlines are brutally early: Early Action and Early Decision close 1 November 2026, most Regular Decision 1 January 2027, and the University of California closes 30 November 2026 - all long before you sit your IB exams.
Immigration costs and admin are real: I-20, SEVIS fee, embassy interview, and post-study work depends on an OPT approval you cannot count on.

ibRecognition.subjectLevelRule: There is no national minimum. Selective universities look at the whole transcript and at HL subject choice rather than at a points threshold. Higher Level subjects are what earn credit; Standard Level rarely does.
ibRecognition.gradeConversion: There is no national IB-to-GPA conversion. Each university reads your IB predicted grades and, later, your final July results directly. The University of California publishes a credit conversion: a full IB Diploma with 30+ points earns 6 quarter units, and each Higher Level exam graded 5, 6 or 7 earns 8 quarter units (5.3 semester units), usually 24 quarter units in total.
notes: Credit for HL 5+ is common but the rules differ at every single university - check the specific university's IB credit page, not a general guide.
Yale states that IB results may be added to an application but cannot replace the required SAT or ACT score.
Harvard will accept IB scores instead of the SAT/ACT only where testing is genuinely unavailable, not as a normal alternative.
Your school sends predicted grades; final results arrive 5-6 July 2027, well after decisions. Offers are effectively made on predictions plus everything else in the file.

portal.name: Common App (most private and many public universities)

deadlines.label: Common App opens for the cycle
deadlines.notes: Common App opened its 2026-27 season on 31 July 2026. You can create an account and draft essays before that; the personal essay rolls over.

deadlines.label: Early Action / Early Decision / Restrictive Early Action
deadlines.notes: Harvard's Restrictive Early Action deadline is 1 November with decisions in mid-December. Most universities that run an early round use the same date.

deadlines.label: University of California application
deadlines.notes: UC uses its own application, not the Common App, and closes earlier than everyone else. UC campuses were open for the fall 2027 application as of September 2026. The fee is 80 USD per campus, 95 USD for international and non-immigrant applicants.

deadlines.label: Regular Decision
deadlines.notes: Harvard's Regular Decision deadline is 1 January with decisions at the end of March. Some universities use 5 or 15 January instead - check each one.

deadlines.label: Early Decision II
deadlines.notes: Grinnell College, for example, uses 5 January for ED II and 15 January for Regular Decision, with financial aid forms due on the same day.

deadlines.label: Reply deadline
deadlines.notes: The national candidates' reply date. Harvard notes that both of its rounds are non-binding, so you can compare offers until 1 May.

steps: From spring 2026, build a list of 8-12 universities in three groups: places that meet full need for internationals, places likely to give you merit money, and one or two you could genuinely afford at full price.
Register for and sit the SAT or ACT in 2026 if any university on your list requires it, and plan a retake date before November.
Create a Common App account when it opens on 31 July 2026, fill in your personal details once, and add your universities.
Ask two teachers and your studievejleder for references in spring 2026, not in October. Your counsellor also uploads the school report and your predicted IB grades.
Write the 650-word personal essay over the summer, then the supplemental essays - Harvard alone asks five 150-word short answers.
Submit early-round applications by 1 November 2026, the UC application by 30 November 2026, and the rest by 1 January 2027, paying each application fee (Harvard's is 95 USD) or requesting a waiver.
Submit financial aid forms - the CSS Profile or the university's own international aid form - by the same deadline as the application, not later.
Decide by 1 May 2027, then wait for the I-20, pay the SEVIS fee and book an embassy appointment in Copenhagen for the F-1 visa.
application.selectionNotes: Holistic review: no published points threshold, no ranking table, no guaranteed entry. Committees read grades and rigour of subjects first, then essays, references, activities and context, and at most universities also your ability to pay. Early Decision is binding - if admitted you must withdraw other applications - and it meaningfully raises your odds, but it removes your ability to compare financial aid offers. Early Action and Restrictive Early Action are non-binding. International admit rates at the most famous universities are in the low single digits; do not build a list out of them.

language.englishTaughtBachelors: Everything. The question is not whether the degree is in English but whether you must prove your English.
language.englishProof: Many universities waive TOEFL/IELTS for students who have been taught in English, which an IB Diploma from an English-medium programme normally demonstrates - but the waiver is not automatic and each university sets its own rule. Check the specific university; where no waiver applies, typical requirements are TOEFL iBT 100+ or IELTS 7.0+ at selective universities. The exact thresholds were not verified for this guide.
notes: Your IB English A Literature or Language and Literature result is the strongest evidence you can offer, but ask each admissions office in writing whether it replaces the test.
Some universities also use the Duolingo English Test. Availability varies year to year.

tuitionEuEea.value: Not applicable - the United States does not have an EU/EEA fee category. As a Dane you pay the international or out-of-state rate everywhere.

tuitionNonEu.value: Private universities: Harvard's published billed cost for 2025-26 was 86,926 USD (tuition 59,320, fees 5,476, housing 13,532, food 8,598), with total billed and unbilled costs of 90,426-95,426 USD plus 4,308 USD health insurance if you are not covered elsewhere. Public universities: UC Berkeley's 2026-27 tuition and fees for a new student are 18,214 USD, but new out-of-state students pay an additional Nonresident Supplemental Tuition of 39,270 USD, so an international first-year pays roughly 57,500 USD in tuition and fees and a total cost of attendance around 94,000 USD in a residence hall.

costs.applicationFee: Harvard 95 USD; University of California 95 USD per campus for international applicants (80 USD for domestic). Most universities charge 50-100 USD per application, and fee waivers exist but are usually aimed at low-income US students.

livingCostMonthly.value: Not published as a monthly figure. American universities publish an annual 'cost of attendance' that already includes housing, food, books, transport and personal expenses - see the tuition figures above. UC Berkeley's 2026-27 estimate for housing and utilities in an off-campus apartment is 14,386 USD for a nine-month academic year, about 1,609 USD a month.

notes: Always read the 'cost of attendance', never the tuition line alone. The COA is also the number financial aid is calculated against.
Health insurance is compulsory and charged separately at most universities. Harvard's was 4,308 USD for 2025-26.
Budget for flights home twice a year; Berkeley allows 0-5,000 USD for transportation and Harvard allows the same range.
The I-901 SEVIS fee is 350 USD for F-1 students, paid before your visa interview.

NOT VERIFIED ON AN OFFICIAL PAGE: the nonimmigrant visa application (MRV) fee is widely reported as 185 USD and a new 250 USD Visa Integrity Fee was introduced by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act with effect from 1 October 2025. We could not fetch travel.state.gov to confirm either figure - check current fees at travel.state.gov before you budget.

funding: Need-based institutional aid. A short list of universities is need-blind for international applicants and meets 100% of assessed need. Harvard states plainly that international students are eligible for exactly the same aid as Americans, that admission is need-blind, and that families earning under 100,000 USD pay nothing, while families up to 200,000 USD have tuition covered. NOT FULLY VERIFIED: widely reported members of this group also include Yale, Princeton, MIT, Amherst, Bowdoin, Dartmouth, Brown, Notre Dame and Washington and Lee - confirm on each university's own financial aid page before you apply.

Need-aware full-need aid. Many strong liberal arts colleges consider your finances when deciding but then meet 100% of need if they admit you. Grinnell College is explicit about this: need-aware for internationals, then 100% of institutionally determined need met.

Merit scholarships. Some universities award merit money regardless of need - Grinnell says outstanding international applicants are considered for merit aid whether or not they apply for need-based help. Merit awards are usually partial, 10,000-30,000 USD a year, and are concentrated at universities outside the top 20.

Athletic scholarships (NCAA). Real but narrow. Division I and II programmes can offer athletic money; Division III, which includes most liberal arts colleges, cannot offer any athletic aid at all. You must register with the NCAA Eligibility Center and be recruited by a coach - you cannot apply for an athletic scholarship the way you apply for a grant. For a Danish IB student this is realistic only in sports where you already compete at national level, typically rowing, swimming, football, handball, golf or tennis.

Danish SU. Danish state education support can in some circumstances follow you abroad for a full degree. Rules are set by Uddannelses- og Forskningsstyrelsen and were not verified for this guide - talk to your studievejleder and check su.dk early, because the application has its own deadlines.
US federal student loans are not available to international students, and most private US loans require a US co-signer.
workRights: On an F-1 visa you may work on campus during your studies, subject to limits set by your university, and off-campus work generally requires prior authorisation. After your degree, Optional Practical Training (OPT) gives up to 12 months of work authorisation directly related to your major, and graduates of approved STEM degrees can apply for a further 24-month extension if the employer is enrolled in E-Verify. You cannot start OPT until USCIS approves Form I-765 and you receive the Employment Authorization Document. Source: https://www.uscis.gov/working-in-the-united-states/students-and-exchange-visitors/optional-practical-training-opt-for-f-1-students
residency: There is no EU-style free movement. After you accept an offer the university issues Form I-20, you pay the I-901 SEVIS fee of 350 USD, complete the DS-160 form, pay the visa fee and attend an interview at the US Embassy in Copenhagen for an F-1 student visa. Bring the SEVIS receipt to the interview - it is required. You may enter the US up to 30 days before your programme starts. Sources: https://www.ice.gov/sevis/i901 and https://studyinthestates.dhs.gov/students/prepare/paying-the-i-901-sevis-fee
housing: Almost all universities house first-year students on campus and many require it. That is a genuine advantage over Europe: you do not hunt for a room, you get assigned one, and the cost is in the published cost of attendance. Harvard's 2025-26 housing and food came to 22,130 USD; Berkeley's residence hall housing and meal plan for 2026-27 are 16,640 USD and 7,000 USD. From year two, many students move off campus, which is where costs and hassle rise - Berkeley budgets 14,386 USD for nine months in an off-campus apartment.
healthcare: Health insurance is compulsory and expensive, and the Danish yellow card and EHIC are worthless in the US. Universities charge their own student health plan unless you can prove equivalent cover - Harvard's was 4,308 USD for 2025-26 and Berkeley's SHIP is 5,066 USD for 2026-27. Private Danish travel or study insurance sometimes qualifies for a waiver, but the university decides and the waiver deadline is usually 1 July. Assume you will pay for the university plan.

institutions.name: Harvard University
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year AB or SB; you declare a concentration in the second year.
institutions.note: Need-blind for internationals and meets 100% of need, which makes it one of the few places where a Danish family on a normal income could actually afford to send a child - but the admit rate is in the low single digits, so treat it as a lottery ticket, not a plan.

institutions.name: Yale University
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA or BS across roughly 80 majors, with a strong residential college system.
institutions.note: Requires the SAT or ACT from every first-year applicant and states explicitly that IB results cannot replace it - so if Yale is on your list, book a test date in 2026.

institutions.name: Massachusetts Institute of Technology
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year SB degrees; everyone takes the same science and maths core in year one.
institutions.note: The most maths-and-physics-intensive undergraduate experience in the US, and widely reported to be need-blind for internationals - verify that on MIT's own student financial services pages, which we could not fetch.

institutions.name: Stanford University
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA/BS on a quarter system, so you take more, shorter courses than at most US universities.
institutions.note: Reported to have reinstated a testing requirement and to be need-aware for internationals - check both on Stanford's own pages, as we could not verify them.

institutions.name: Amherst College
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA with an open curriculum - no distribution requirements at all beyond your major.
institutions.note: About 1,900 students and consistently named as one of the very few liberal arts colleges that is need-blind for international applicants and meets full need; it is as selective as an Ivy, so apply alongside, not instead of, less selective colleges.

institutions.name: Bowdoin College
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA, about 1,800 students, small classes and no graduate students competing for attention.
institutions.note: Regularly listed among the need-blind, full-need colleges for internationals; coastal Maine is beautiful and genuinely remote, which suits some Danish students and not others.

institutions.name: Grinnell College
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA with an individually advised curriculum; roughly 1,700 students and an unusually high international share.
institutions.note: One of the most realistic targets on this list: need-aware for internationals but then meets 100% of assessed need, and also considers internationals for merit awards. ED I 15 November, ED II 5 January, RD 15 January - aid forms due the same day.

institutions.name: Macalester College
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA with an explicit internationalist mission; around 2,000 students in a real city.
institutions.note: Long-standing reputation for recruiting and funding international students, and being in the Twin Cities means jobs, flights and a Scandinavian-heavy Midwest that feels less foreign than you would expect. Confirm its current international aid policy directly.

institutions.name: Colby College
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA, about 2,200 students, with a January term for one intensive project.
institutions.note: Reported to award substantial credit for a strong full IB Diploma - worth asking the registrar directly, because a year of credit changes the total cost of the degree more than any scholarship will.

institutions.name: New York University
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year degrees across separate schools - you apply to one school, such as Stern or Tisch, not to NYU in general.
institutions.note: Enormous international intake and campuses in Abu Dhabi and Shanghai, but it is famously need-aware and does not meet full need for most internationals; go in expecting to pay a large share of a very high New York cost of living.

institutions.name: University of Michigan-Ann Arbor
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year degrees across 19 schools, with a large liberal arts college at the centre.
institutions.note: A top-tier public university with a classic American campus experience; out-of-state and international tuition is close to private-university levels and institutional aid for internationals is limited.

institutions.name: University of California, Berkeley
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year BA/BS; you apply to a college within Berkeley, and some majors are capped.
institutions.note: Apply through the UC application by 30 November 2026, not the Common App. For 2026-27 a new international pays 18,214 USD of tuition and fees plus 39,270 USD Nonresident Supplemental Tuition, and UC gives essentially no need-based aid to internationals - but the UC system's published IB credit rules are the most generous and transparent in the country.

institutions.name: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year degrees; you apply to a specific major, and engineering and computer science are far harder to enter than the university overall.
institutions.note: A serious engineering and computing school at a public-university price, with a huge international community and a less theatrical admissions process than the private universities.

institutions.name: Arizona State University
institutions.englishBachelors: Four-year degrees across more than 350 undergraduate programmes, with published admission criteria rather than holistic review.
institutions.note: The honest 'realistic' entry on this list: admission is largely criteria-based rather than a lottery, automatic merit awards for international students are published in advance, and the total cost sits well below the private universities.
